text: समुद्र तट का रंग इस पर टिका है कि उसकी रेत किससे बनी है, और यह आस-पास की चट्टानों और जीवों पर निर्भर करता है। ज़्यादातर काली रेत [[basalt|बेसाल्ट]] नाम की गहरी ज्वालामुखी चट्टान से आती है। जब [[lava|लावा]] समुद्र में गिरता है, या लहरें पुरानी लावा चट्टानों पर थपेड़े मारती हैं, तो चट्टान टूटकर नन्हे काले दानों में बदल जाती है।

कुछ काली रेत भारी, गहरे [[mineral|खनिजों]] से बनी होती है, जिन्हें लहरें और धाराएँ हल्के दानों से अलग करके किनारे पर जमा कर देती हैं। हल्के और सुनहरे तट आमतौर पर क्वार्ट्ज़ से बने होते हैं, जो एक मज़बूत, हल्के रंग का खनिज है। चकाचौंध करने वाले सफ़ेद उष्णकटिबंधीय तट अक्सर पिसे हुए मूँगे और सीपियों से बने होते हैं।

sec.t:
काले तट सबसे ज़्यादा ज्वालामुखी वाले द्वीपों पर मिलते हैं। समुद्र में खड़ा [[@volcano|ज्वालामुखी]] नई चट्टान जोड़ता रहता है, और लहरें उसे तोड़ना कभी बंद नहीं करतीं। हवाई के बिग आइलैंड पर पुनालुउ बीच अपनी गहरी काली रेत के लिए मशहूर है, जहाँ हरे समुद्री कछुए अक्सर किनारे आकर आराम करते हैं। 2018 में किलाउआ ज्वालामुखी का लावा समुद्र में बहा, और कुछ ही महीनों में पोहोइकी पर एक बिल्कुल नया काली रेत वाला तट बन गया।

[[@iceland|आइसलैंड]] में रेनिसफ़्यारा पर काली रेत है, गरजती लहरें हैं, और चट्टानों के साथ बेसाल्ट के ऊँचे खंभे हैं। काली रेत धूप सोखती है, इसलिए धूप वाले दिन यह इतनी गरम हो सकती है कि नंगे पैर जल जाएँ, बगल की हल्की रेत से कहीं ज़्यादा गरम।

मालदीव और लक्षद्वीप जैसी जगहों की चमकीली सफ़ेद रेत ज़्यादातर समुद्री जीवों के कंकालों से बनी है: टूटे मूँगे, सीपियाँ और नन्हे जीवों के सख़्त टुकड़े। इसका बड़ा हिस्सा तोता मछली बनाती है। मूँगा चट्टानों में रहने वाली ये रंग-बिरंगी मछलियाँ मूँगे पर उगे शैवाल खाने के लिए उसके टुकड़े काट लेती हैं। वे गले में मौजूद दाँतों से सख़्त मूँगे को पीसती हैं और महीन रेत बनाकर बाहर निकाल देती हैं।

एक बड़ी तोता मछली एक साल में सैकड़ों किलो मूँगे को रेत में बदल सकती है। तो एक सेहतमंद [[@coral-reefs|मूँगा चट्टान]] पास के तटों को ताज़ा रेत पहुँचाती रहती है।

हवाई के पापाकोलेआ बीच पर रेत जैतूनी हरी है। यह ओलिवीन से आती है, जो वहाँ की ज्वालामुखी चट्टान का एक हरा खनिज है। यह दूसरे दानों से भारी है, इसलिए तट पर जमा हो जाता है। बहामास के हार्बर आइलैंड और बरमूडा पर तट गुलाबी दिखते हैं, क्योंकि फ़ोरामिनिफ़ेरा नाम के लाल खोल वाले नन्हे जीव सफ़ेद रेत में मिल जाते हैं।

फिर भी ज़्यादातर तट सुनहरे या हल्के भूरे होते हैं। क्वार्ट्ज़ सख़्त है और आसानी से नहीं घुलता, इसलिए दूसरे खनिज घिस जाने के बाद यही बचता है। हज़ारों सालों में नदियाँ पहाड़ों से दाने समुद्र तक लाती हैं, और [[@waves-how|लहरें]] उन्हें आकार और वज़न के हिसाब से छाँट देती हैं। तट की रेत की हर मुट्ठी इस बात का रिकॉर्ड है कि वह कहाँ से आई। आवर्धक लेंस से ध्यान से देखो, तो शायद तुम्हें साफ़ क्वार्ट्ज़, काले कण, गुलाबी सीपियों के टुकड़े और कहीं-कहीं अभ्रक की चमक दिखे, सब अलग-अलग जगहों से आए हुए।

text: ब्लैक होल वह जगह है जहाँ इतना सारा [[matter|पदार्थ]] इतनी छोटी जगह में ठूँस दिया गया हो कि उसका [[@gravity-fall|गुरुत्वाकर्षण]] रोशनी तक को बाहर नहीं निकलने देता। इसके किनारे को इवेंट होराइज़न कहते हैं। इसे पार कर लिया, तो बाहर लौटने का कोई रास्ता नहीं, रोशनी की रफ़्तार से भी नहीं।

तुम्हारे साथ क्या होगा, यह ब्लैक होल के आकार पर निर्भर करता है। सूरज से कुछ गुना भारी एक छोटा ब्लैक होल किनारे तक पहुँचने से पहले ही तुम्हें खींचकर एक लंबी, पतली डोरी बना देगा। वैज्ञानिक सच में इसे "स्पेगेटीफ़िकेशन" कहते हैं। सूरज से लाखों गुना भारी एक विशाल ब्लैक होल तुम्हें बिना कुछ महसूस कराए किनारे के पार निकल जाने देगा। उसके बाद क्या होगा, यह पक्के तौर पर कोई नहीं जानता।

sec.t:
जितना पास जाओ, गुरुत्वाकर्षण उतना ताक़तवर होता जाता है। पैरों के बल गिरते हुए तुम्हारे पैर सिर से ज़्यादा ज़ोर से खिंचेंगे। धरती पर यह फ़र्क इतना छोटा है कि महसूस ही नहीं होता। चाँद का यही खिंचाव-फ़र्क समुद्र में [[@tides|ज्वार]] उठाता है।

छोटे ब्लैक होल के पास यह फ़र्क बहुत बड़ा होता है। तुम्हारा शरीर लंबाई में खिंचेगा और अगल-बगल से दबेगा, जैसे ट्यूब से टूथपेस्ट निकलता है। यह किनारे से सैकड़ों किलोमीटर पहले ही हो जाएगा, इसलिए तुम इवेंट होराइज़न को पास से कभी देख ही नहीं पाओगे।

ब्लैक होल अंतरिक्ष के साथ-साथ समय को भी मोड़ देते हैं। यह विचार [[@einstein|आइंस्टाइन]] के गुरुत्वाकर्षण के सिद्धांत से आता है। गुरुत्वाकर्षण जितना ताक़तवर, दूर की घड़ियों के मुकाबले घड़ियाँ उतनी धीमी चलती हैं।

तो सुरक्षित दूरी से देख रहे किसी दोस्त को कुछ अजीब दिखेगा। किनारे के पास पहुँचते हुए तुम धीमे, और धीमे गिरते दिखोगे, और फिर वहीं जम जाओगे। तुम्हारी रोशनी खिंचकर ज़्यादा लाल और मद्धम होती जाएगी, जब तक तुम दिखना बंद न हो जाओ। पर तुम्हारी तरफ़ से देखो, तो तुम सीधे अंदर गिर जाओगे।

sec.h: सबसे पास वाला कितनी दूर है?
sec.t:
ग़लती से किसी में गिर जाने का कोई ख़तरा नहीं है। सबसे पास के जाने-पहचाने ब्लैक होलों में से एक, गाया BH1, 2022 में लगभग 1,560 [[lightyear|प्रकाश-वर्ष]] दूर मिला। आज वहाँ से चली रोशनी 1,500 से ज़्यादा साल तक धरती पर नहीं पहुँचेगी। सैजिटेरियस A* इससे कहीं दूर है, हमसे लगभग 27,000 प्रकाश-वर्ष।

खगोलशास्त्री मानते हैं कि हमारी आकाशगंगा में लगभग 10 करोड़ ब्लैक होल हो सकते हैं। ज़्यादातर अदृश्य हैं, क्योंकि उनके पास कुछ भी अंदर नहीं गिर रहा जो उन्हें चमका सके।

sec.t:
हमारे सबसे अच्छे सिद्धांत कहते हैं कि अंदर की हर चीज़ केंद्र की ओर गिरती है, जहाँ पदार्थ कुचलकर अनंत घनत्व वाले एक बिंदु में बदल जाता है, जिसे सिंगुलैरिटी कहते हैं। ज़्यादातर भौतिक विज्ञानी मानते हैं कि यह जवाब पूरा सच नहीं, बल्कि इस बात का इशारा है कि वहाँ हमारे सिद्धांत टूट जाते हैं। गुरुत्वाकर्षण को नन्हे कणों की भौतिकी से जोड़ने वाला कोई सिद्धांत शायद इसे समझा सके, पर अभी तक किसी के पास ऐसा सिद्धांत नहीं है।

इतना हम जानते हैं कि ब्लैक होल असली हैं। 2019 में खगोलशास्त्रियों ने M87 आकाशगंगा में एक ब्लैक होल की पहली तस्वीर जारी की, और 2022 में सैजिटेरियस A* की तस्वीर खींची। दोनों एक काले बीच के चारों ओर चमकते नारंगी छल्लों जैसे दिखते हैं।

और सबसे अजीब बात? बहुत-से ब्लैक होल उन विशाल तारों के बचे हुए केंद्र हैं जो फट गए थे। इसीलिए उनकी कहानी [[@star-life-cycle|तारे कैसे जीते और मरते हैं]] से शुरू होती है।

text: Even in the busiest Indian city, you can spot a dozen kinds of birds without leaving home. The most common are the house crow, the common myna, the rock pigeon and the rose-ringed parakeet. Look up and you'll see black kites circling. Listen and you'll hear red-vented bulbuls, Asian koels and, in many places, house sparrows.

With a little patience, you may also find purple sunbirds sipping [[nectar|nectar]], spotted doves on rooftops, white-throated kingfishers on wires and oriental magpie robins singing from walls. Cities have water, trees, food scraps and plenty of ledges for nesting, so many birds do very well in them.

st.prompt: Which of these city birds builds no nest of its own?

options.t: The Asian koel
The house crow
The common myna

st.reveal: The female koel lays her eggs in a crow's nest, usually while the male distracts the crows. The crows then feed and raise the koel chicks as if they were their own. This trick is called brood parasitism.

d.try: Sit by a window or on a balcony for ten minutes in the early morning and write down every bird you see or hear. Draw a quick sketch or note its colour and size. Do it again in the evening and see whether the list changes. Over a week, you'll have your own city bird count.
myth: Pigeons in Indian cities are native wild birds that have always lived there.

City pigeons come from the rock dove, a wild bird of cliffs. They were tamed thousands of years ago, and today's city flocks are mostly the descendants of tame pigeons gone wild. Building ledges are their new cliffs.

sec.t:
The house crow is grey around the neck and very bold. [[@crow-smart|Crows]] are clever. They learn which houses throw out scraps and at what time, and they remember faces of people who have chased them. Common mynas are brown with yellow beaks and yellow patches around the eyes. They walk rather than hop, and they chatter constantly.

Rock pigeons gather wherever people drop grain. Rose-ringed parakeets are bright green, with long tails and red beaks. They screech as they fly past in flocks at dawn and dusk. Some escaped pet parakeets now live wild in London and other European cities, where people are often surprised to see a [[tropical|tropical]] parrot in winter.

Look up over [[@delhi|Delhi]] and you'll often see dozens of birds soaring in slow circles. These are black kites, brown birds of prey with forked tails. They feed on scraps from markets, meat shops and rubbish dumps, and they sometimes snatch food from people's hands.

Kites are often hurt by sharp kite-flying strings, especially around festivals like Independence Day and Makar Sankranti. In Delhi, a pair of brothers have spent years rescuing injured kites in their small basement. Their story became the documentary film All That Breathes, which was nominated for an Oscar in 2023.

Older Indians remember house [[@sparrows|sparrows]] hopping into kitchens. In some big cities, they became much harder to find. Modern buildings have fewer gaps for nests, gardens have fewer insects for chicks to eat, and shops sell grain in sealed packets.

The State of India's Birds report in 2023 found that sparrows were doing fine across India as a whole, but had dropped in several large cities. In 2012, Delhi made the house sparrow its state bird to draw attention to it. World Sparrow Day is on 20 March, and many families now put up small nest boxes and water bowls.

You don't need special gear to start. A notebook, a window and some quiet time are enough. Binoculars help, and a field guide or a free app can tell you what you are seeing. [[@birdwatching|Birdwatching]] is one of the easiest hobbies to begin, because birds are almost everywhere.

Scientists also welcome help. Every count you add to a citizen science website like eBird shows researchers which birds are doing well and which are disappearing. A child's balcony list in Pune or Patna can end up in a national report.

text: Starting birdwatching is simple. Pick a quiet spot, sit still and look and listen. Early morning is best, because birds are most active then. Note what you see: its size, colour, shape, beak and how it moves. Then use a field guide, a book of bird pictures, or a free app to work out its name.

You don't need special gear to begin. A notebook and pencil are enough. Later, a pair of binoculars will help you see details like eye colour or wing stripes. The most important skill is patience. Birds hide, flit and fly off, and the more time you spend watching, the more you notice.

st.prompt: When is usually the best time of day to see the most birds?

options.t: Early morning, soon after sunrise
Midday, when it is brightest
Late at night

st.reveal: Most birds are busiest in the first few hours after sunrise, feeding and singing after the night. In hot places like much of India, they rest in the shade during the middle of the day. Evenings are good too, as birds feed again and fly to roost.

You can start with nothing but your eyes, ears and a notebook. Many common birds are easy to see in parks and gardens. Binoculars help later, and a simple, cheap pair is fine for beginners.

sec.t:
Experienced birdwatchers, often called birders, start with a few simple questions. How big is it, compared to a sparrow, a myna or a crow? What shape is its beak: short and thick for cracking seeds, long and thin for sipping [[nectar|nectar]], hooked for tearing meat? What colours and patterns stand out?

Behaviour helps too. Does it hop or walk? Does it climb up tree trunks or hover in the air? Does it fly in a straight line or in swoops? A bird that wags its tail as it walks on a lawn may be a wagtail. One sitting very still on a wire, then diving into water, may be a kingfisher.

When Salim Ali was about ten, in Bombay, he shot a small bird with a yellow patch on its throat. Curious, he took it to the Bombay Natural History Society. A staff member there identified it as a yellow-throated sparrow and showed him drawers full of stuffed birds.

That visit changed his life. Salim Ali went on to survey birds across India and wrote The Book of Indian Birds, first published in 1941, which is still read today. He helped protect places like Keoladeo National Park in Bharatpur, a [[@wetlands|wetland]] famous for winter birds. India now marks 12 November, his birthday, as National Bird Day.

Birders do more than enjoy the view. Their counts help scientists track which birds are thriving and which are in trouble. In the United States, the Christmas Bird Count has run since 1900. The Great Backyard Bird Count began in 1998 and now takes place every February around the world.

In India, schools, colleges and families take part in Campus Bird Counts and Great Backyard Bird Counts, and they upload lists to eBird, a free website and app. These millions of lists help researchers write big reports, such as the State of India's Birds. This kind of shared science is a good example of [[@data-science|data science]] in action.

The birds come first. Never chase birds, touch nests or get too close to chicks. Stay on paths, keep quiet and don't play recorded calls over and over to lure birds out, as this can stress them, especially in nesting season.

When you're new, it's fine to get things wrong. Even expert birders argue over tricky warblers and distant hawks. Join a local bird walk if you can. They are often free, and an experienced birder can teach you more in a morning than a book can in a month.

text: A pufferfish puffs up by swallowing water, fast. It pumps water into a stomach that can stretch to many times its normal size. In about 15 seconds, a long, ordinary-looking fish becomes a round ball two or three times bigger.

This makes it hard for a [[predator|predator]] to swallow. Trying to gulp it down would be like trying to bite into a football. Many pufferfish also have spines that stick out when they inflate, and most carry a deadly poison. Together, these defences mean very few animals try to eat them twice.

st.prompt: How does a pufferfish make itself so big?

options.t: It gulps lots of water into a very stretchy stomach
It fills its body with gas made by its blood
It grows extra fat in a few seconds

st.reveal: A pufferfish pumps water into its stomach with fast mouth movements. The stomach can stretch enormously, and the fish has no ribs to get in the way. When the danger is over, it spits the water out.

d.try: See how a stretchy pouch makes you big. Slide a deflated balloon inside a sock, leaving the neck sticking out. Slowly blow up the balloon and watch the sock stretch. A pufferfish's skin and stomach work a bit like the sock and balloon together.
myth: Pufferfish should be helped to puff up because it is fun to watch.

Puffing is a stress response and uses a lot of energy. Divers and aquarium keepers are asked never to make pufferfish inflate, and lifting one out of the water can make it gulp air instead, which can harm it.

sec.t:
A pufferfish's stomach is folded like an accordion. When it is scared, it opens its mouth and throat and uses strong muscles to pump in water, gulp after gulp. A special valve stops the water flowing back out.

To make room, the fish has unusual skin and bones. Its skin is very stretchy and folded. It has no ribs, which in most fish would hold the body in shape and block the stomach from swelling. Its spine can bend into a curve to make space too.

When the danger has passed, it pushes the water out through its mouth and shrinks back. Puffing takes a lot of energy, and a pufferfish may take hours to fully recover.

{{story:ocean-sunfish}}

Most pufferfish carry tetrodotoxin, one of the strongest natural poisons known. It blocks the signals that nerves use to talk to muscles. A tiny amount can stop someone breathing. It is often described as more than a thousand times deadlier than cyanide.

The fish doesn't make the poison itself. [[bacteria|Bacteria]] make it, and the pufferfish builds it up by eating shellfish and other animals that carry those bacteria. Pufferfish raised in tanks on clean food are often not poisonous at all.

The same poison is found in blue-ringed octopuses and some newts. This is a [[@snakes-venom|poison]], not a [[venom|venom]], because it harms you if you eat it rather than if it bites you.

In [[@japan-culture|Japan]], pufferfish is a famous and expensive dish called fugu. Only specially trained chefs may prepare it. They study for years and pass difficult tests, learning to remove the poisonous liver, ovaries and skin.

Even so, a few people get sick each year, usually after trying to prepare it at home. In parts of India, the US and elsewhere, people also catch pufferfish, and doctors warn that eating them without expert preparation can be deadly.

Pufferfish have four large teeth fused into a strong beak, two on top and two below. That is where their family name comes from: *Tetraodontidae* means "four teeth". They use the beak to crack crabs, clams, snails and sea urchins. Some [[species|species]] nibble on [[@coral-reefs|coral reefs]], scraping off the tiny animals and [[algae|algae]] that grow there.

The teeth never stop growing. Crunching hard shells keeps them worn down, a bit like a rabbit's teeth.

In 1995, divers off Amami Ōshima in southern Japan found strange circles in the sand on the seabed, about 2 m across, with ridges and grooves like a flower. For years, nobody knew who made them.

Around 2011, scientists finally filmed the answer. A small male white-spotted pufferfish, only about 12 cm long, swims back and forth for about a week, flapping its fins to shape the sand. Females visit the circle and lay eggs in the middle.

The patterns are so neat and regular that people once guessed they were made by humans. Nature is full of such patterns, from the spiral of a snail to the six sides of a honeycomb, as the maths of [[@maths-nature-shells|nature's shells]] shows.

text: Very rarely. There are more than 500 kinds of shark, and only a handful have ever been known to bite people without being provoked. In 2025, scientists recorded 65 such bites worldwide, and 9 of them were deadly. More people die each year from lightning or bee stings than from sharks.

Meanwhile, people kill an enormous number of sharks, roughly 80 million a year, for their fins, meat and oil, or by catching them by accident. For sharks, people are far more dangerous than the other way round.

st.prompt: In the USA, which kills more people in a typical year?

options.t: Lightning
Sharks

st.reveal: Lightning kills about 20 people a year in the USA. Sharks usually kill one or none. You are also far more likely to be hurt driving to the beach than in the water.

d.try: Draw a shark to scale on a long strip of paper. A whale shark can reach about 18 m, longer than a school bus or a Mumbai local train coach. A dwarf lanternshark is about 20 cm, the length of your forearm. Mark both, then add yourself to see where you fit.
myth: Sharks must keep swimming all the time or they will die.

Some sharks, such as great whites, do need to keep moving so water flows over their gills. But many others, like nurse sharks, can rest on the seabed and pump water over their gills while lying still.
facts: the whale shark, up to about 18 m

sec.t:
Most bites come from three [[species|species]]: the great white, the tiger shark and the bull shark. Bull sharks can live in rivers as well as the sea, and have been found far up the Mississippi and the Amazon.

Scientists think most bites are mistakes. A shark may take a test bite of a surfer paddling on a board, which from below looks a bit like a seal. Many bites happen in murky water near the shore, and the shark often lets go and swims off. Florida usually has the most bites of anywhere, simply because so many people surf and swim there.

Experts at the International Shark Attack File suggest a few simple habits. Swim close to the shore, near lifeguards, and with other people. Avoid the water at dawn and dusk, when many sharks feed, and stay out of murky water or places where people are fishing. Shiny jewellery can flash like fish scales, so leave it on the sand.

Shark bites are very rare on India's beaches. The bigger dangers there are strong currents and rough [[monsoon|monsoon]] waves, which is why swimming is banned on many Indian beaches during the monsoon.

Sharks have an excellent sense of [[@nose-smell|smell]]. Some can notice blood in the water at about one part in a million, roughly a drop in a large tub of water. The old claim that they can smell a single drop from a kilometre away is an exaggeration.

They also have senses we lack. Tiny jelly-filled pores on their snouts detect the weak electric signals given off by living animals, even ones hiding in sand. A line of [[sensor|sensors]] down each side feels movement in the water. A hammerhead's wide head spreads these sensors out, like a metal detector sweeping the seabed.

sec.h: Why sharks need us more than we fear them
sec.t:
Sharks are ancient. Their ancestors appeared more than 400 million years ago, before trees grew on land, and they have survived several mass extinctions. As [[@coral-reefs|hunters at the top of the food chain]], they help keep reefs and seas in balance by eating sick and weak animals.

Today, many shark species are in trouble. They grow slowly and have few young, so heavy fishing hits them hard. India made the whale shark, the biggest fish in the sea at up to about 18 metres long, a protected animal in 2001. Fishers in Gujarat, who once caught them, now often cut their nets to free any that get tangled. Gujarat's government pays them for the damaged nets, and hundreds of whale sharks have been set free this way.

text: Bricks are made from clay, the sticky, fine-grained part of soil. Workers dig it, mix it with water until it is like thick dough, and press it into rectangular moulds. The soft bricks are tipped out in rows to dry in the sun for days or weeks.

Then comes the fire. The dried bricks are stacked inside a [[kiln|kiln]] and heated to around 1,000 °C, several times hotter than a kitchen oven. The heat changes the clay for good. Tiny grains melt at the edges and fuse together, turning the brick into a hard ceramic, like a clay pot. After cooling, the bricks are ready to be laid with mortar into walls.

st.prompt: Most bricks come out of the kiln red. What gives them that colour?

options.t: Iron in the clay, changed by the heat
Red paint brushed on before firing
Smoke from the fire staining them

st.reveal: Most clays contain a little iron. Heated with plenty of air in the kiln, the iron turns into red iron oxide, the same stuff as rust. Clay low in iron fires to cream or yellow.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Brick.

d.try: Make two mini bricks from damp garden soil or clay pressed into an ice-cube tray. Leave them in the sun for a few days until hard. Then put one in a bowl of water and watch what happens. Sun-dried bricks soften in water, which is why kiln-fired bricks were such a big step.
myth: A brick is just mud that has dried hard.

That's true for sun-dried bricks. Fired bricks are different, because the heat of the kiln changes the clay into a kind of stone-like ceramic that will never turn back into mud, even after centuries of rain.

sec.t:
In much of South Asia, bricks are still fired in tall chimney kilns standing in fields at the edge of towns. Workers stack thousands of dried bricks in rows, with gaps for hot air. Coal or other fuel is fed in from the top, and the fire slowly moves around the kiln over days, so some bricks heat up while others cool.

Big factories elsewhere use long tunnel kilns. The bricks ride slowly through on carts, passing through warm, hot and cooling zones, like a very slow train. Most factories now shape the clay by squeezing it through a nozzle, a bit like toothpaste, then slicing it into bricks with wires.

Sizes are standard today too. A common modern Indian brick is about 19 cm long, 9 cm wide and 9 cm high. With a centimetre of mortar around it, that makes a neat 20 by 10 by 10, which helps builders plan walls quickly.

India makes more bricks than any country except China, from tens of thousands of kilns. Many burn coal and give off smoke and dust. Around cities like Delhi, brick kilns are one of the sources of winter [[@air-pollution|air pollution]]. Newer "zigzag" kilns guide the hot air along a winding path, which burns fuel more completely and cuts smoke.

Kiln work is hard and hot. Many workers are migrants who come for the dry season with their families. Some are trapped by debts to kiln owners, and children are sometimes made to work. The government and charities have tried to stop this, with mixed success.

Builders are trying alternatives. Fly ash bricks use ash from coal power stations, mixed with lime and sand, and need no firing. Compressed earth blocks are pressed hard in a machine and dried. Concrete blocks, made with [[@cement-concrete|cement]], are cheaper to lay in some places.

Still, fired brick lasts. Old Indian forts, British railway stations and the red brick buildings of American cities like Boston have stood for well over a century. Since clay comes from the [[@soil-made|soil]] under our feet, the oldest building material is also one of the easiest to find.

text: A swing is a [[pendulum|pendulum]]: a weight hanging from a fixed point, free to rock back and forth. Left alone, it slowly loses energy to air and [[friction|friction]] and comes to a stop.

When you pump, you add energy back in. Sitting down, you lean back and stretch your legs out as you swing forward, then sit up and tuck your legs under as you swing back. Standing up, you crouch at the high points and stand up tall as you whoosh through the bottom.
Each time, you shift your body's weight closer to or farther from the top bar, at just the right moments. That small push of your own muscles, timed with the swing, adds up to bigger and bigger arcs.

st.prompt: Two friends sit on identical swings, one much heavier than the other. They are pulled back the same amount and let go. Whose swing goes back and forth faster?

options.t: Neither, they keep the same time
The heavier friend's
The lighter friend's

st.reveal: For a pendulum, the time of each swing depends on the length of the rope and the pull of gravity, not on the weight hanging from it. So both friends swing in step, at least until one of them starts pumping.

myth: You can only go high on a swing if somebody pushes you.
A rider can pump a swing from standing still, just by moving their body at the right moments. A push helps get started, but good pumping alone can take you very high.
facts: the length of the ropes, not the rider's weight
about 53 kg, swings up to about 65 km/h

sec.t:
Around 1600, the Italian scientist [[@galileo|Galileo]] noticed something odd about pendulums. A popular story says he watched a lamp swinging in Pisa cathedral and timed it with his pulse. Whether or not that happened, his experiments showed that a pendulum keeps nearly the same [[rhythm|rhythm]], whether it swings wide or small.

The time depends on the length of the rope. A swing with ropes about 2 metres long takes roughly 2.8 seconds to go forward and back. A longer swing is slower. The rider's weight makes almost no difference, because [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] pulls harder on heavier things but they are harder to move by the same amount.

Pendulums keep time so well that, for nearly 300 years, the best [[@clocks|clocks]] in the world used them.

Seated pumping is a little different. When you lean back and kick your legs forward, your body rotates around the seat. That twisting pushes on the ropes and gives the swing a small extra shove in the direction it is already going.

The timing is everything. Lean back too early or too late and you fight the swing instead of helping it. Children usually learn the rhythm by feel, long before anyone explains it. Physicists have written whole research papers about it.

sec.h: Festival swings and a flying incense burner
sec.t:
Swings are part of festivals across India. In the [[monsoon|monsoon]], during Teej, swings are hung from tree branches and decorated with flowers. In Kerala, swings called oonjal are put up for Onam. Many stories show the young Krishna on a swing.

In Spain, the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela has the Botafumeiro, a giant silver-coloured incense burner of about 53 kg hanging from ropes about 20 metres long. A team of men called tiraboleiros pull on the rope in rhythm, shortening it at the bottom of each swing and letting it out at the top. Within a few minutes it swings almost from wall to wall, reaching about 65 km/h. It is exactly the standing-pumping trick, done by a team.

The same timing trick turns up everywhere. Pumping a swing is a cousin of bouncing on a [[@how-trampoline|trampoline]]: in both, a well-timed push at the right moment adds a little energy each time, until you are flying.

text: A radio wave is a ripple of electric and magnetic energy. It belongs to the same family as visible light, but its waves are much longer, so our eyes can't see it. Like light, it travels at about 3 lakh kilometres a second and needs no air at all.

To send a radio signal, a transmitter makes [[electron|electrons]] rush up and down a metal aerial millions of times a second. That shaking sends ripples spreading outwards. Far away, the ripples reach another aerial and make its electrons shake in the same [[rhythm|rhythm]]. The receiver picks out that tiny shake and turns it back into sound, pictures or data.

st.prompt: Mission controllers send a radio message to a rover on the Moon. Roughly how long does it take to arrive?

options.t: About a second
About an hour
About a day

st.reveal: Radio waves travel at the speed of light, about 3 lakh kilometres every second. The Moon is about 3.8 lakh kilometres away, so the message takes a little over a second. A message to Mars can take anywhere from about 3 to 22 minutes.

The sound usually fades or turns to hiss, because the metal box blocks the radio waves from reaching the aerial. Try a plastic box too and compare.
myth: Radio waves travel through the air, so they can't work in space.
Radio waves need nothing to travel through. They cross empty space more easily than air, which is how NASA still talks to the Voyager spacecraft beyond the planets.

sec.t:
Scientists call the whole family of these waves the electromagnetic [[spectrum|spectrum]]. At one end are gamma rays and [[@x-rays|X-rays]], with waves smaller than an [[atom|atom]]. In the middle is the narrow band of light we can see. At the far end are radio waves, which can be as short as a grain of rice or longer than a football field.

Each station sends its waves at its own [[frequency|frequency]], the number of ripples per second. When you turn a radio's dial, you are choosing which frequency to listen to and ignoring the rest. An FM station at 100 megahertz is sending 100 million ripples every second.

sec.h: Carrying a voice on a wave
Bose, Marconi and the first signals
sec.t:
In 1887 and 1888, the German scientist Heinrich Hertz showed in his laboratory that these invisible waves were real. A few years later, in 1895, [[@jagadish-bose|Jagadish Chandra Bose]] gave a public demonstration in Calcutta. He sent very short radio waves, now called microwaves, across a hall and through walls to set off a bell. He chose not to patent most of his work.

Around the same time, the Italian inventor Guglielmo Marconi turned radio into a business. In 1901 his team reported receiving a signal sent across the Atlantic Ocean, from Cornwall in England to Newfoundland. Ships soon carried radios, and in 1912 the sinking *Titanic* used one to call for help. In India, regular broadcasting began in the 1920s, and the national broadcaster took the name All India Radio in 1936.

Stars, [[@galaxies|galaxies]] and clouds of gas send out radio waves too. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] catch them with giant dish-shaped aerials. Near Pune, the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope uses 30 dishes, each 45 metres across, spread over about 25 kilometres of farmland.

Radio waves also travel the other way. NASA's Deep Space Network sends commands to the [[@voyager|Voyager probes]], launched in 1977 and now more than 20 billion kilometres from Earth. Their reply, far weaker than a phone signal by the time it reaches us, takes about a day to arrive. Giant dishes in California, Spain and Australia take turns listening, so one of them always faces the right part of the sky.

text: Nobody knows who invented the wheel. There was no single inventor whose name was written down. What [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] do know is *when* wheels for carrying things started to appear: around 3500 BCE, about 5,500 years ago.

At almost the same moment, wheels show up in [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], the land of the [[@first-cities|first cities]] in present-day Iraq, in the grasslands north of the Black Sea, and in central Europe. A clay pot found at Bronocice in Poland, made about 3500 BCE, has a drawing of what looks like a four-wheeled wagon. Some experts think the idea spread very quickly from one place. Others think it was worked out more than once.

sec.t:
In 2002, archaeologists working in the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia found a wooden wheel preserved in the wet ground. It is about 5,000 years old and as wide as a child's arm span, made from ash planks. The axle found with it was made from oak. Waterlogged mud kept out the [[bacteria|bacteria]] that would normally rot wood away.

Early wheels were solid discs, heavy and slow. Around 2000 BCE, people near the Ural Mountains began building light wheels with spokes for fast [[@wheel-to-chariot|war chariots]]. Spoked wheels soon spread across Asia and Europe. A spoked wheel is far lighter than a solid one of the same size, so a pair of horses could pull a chariot at a gallop. Iron rims came later, to stop the wooden edges wearing away on stony tracks.

At Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and other [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]], archaeologists have dug up small clay models of bullock carts, along with tiny clay wheels. They show that people in the Indus Valley were using carts by around 2500 BCE. Carts very much like them still roll along Indian village roads, pulled by bullocks at a walking pace.

Wheels also turned up in art and faith. The Sun Temple at [[@konark|Konark]] in Odisha, built in the 1200s, is designed as the chariot of the Sun god, with 24 huge stone wheels carved into its sides. India's national flag carries the Ashoka Chakra, a wheel with 24 spokes.

The [[@pottery|potter's wheel]] may be even older than the cart wheel, though it turned flat, like a spinning table. Later came water wheels for grinding grain, the spinning wheel for thread, and gears inside clocks.

Wheels did not suit everyone. In the deserts of the Middle East, [[@camels|camels]] replaced carts for many centuries, because they needed no roads. Yet today wheels are almost everywhere, from your school bus to the spinning parts inside a hard disk. Each one depends on the same old trick: cutting down [[@friction|friction]] by rolling instead of dragging.

sec.t:
ट्रे की आम बर्फ़ धुँधली होती है। जब पानी बाहर से अंदर की ओर जमता है, तो उसमें घुली हवा और [[mineral|खनिज]] बीच की ओर धकेले जाते हैं और नन्हे बुलबुलों के रूप में फँस जाते हैं। धुँधली बर्फ़ सफ़ेद दिखती है और आसानी से चटक जाती है।

मूर्तिकार खास मशीनें इस्तेमाल करते हैं, जो पानी को नीचे से ऊपर की ओर धीरे-धीरे जमाती हैं, जबकि एक पंप पानी को चलाता रहता है। बुलबुले ऊपर उठकर निकल जाते हैं। कुछ दिनों में खिड़की के काँच जितनी साफ़ सिल्ली तैयार हो जाती है। रोशनी सीधे आर-पार निकल जाती है, और पीछे से रोशनी डालो तो तैयार मूर्ति जगमगाती-सी लगती है।

उत्तरी स्वीडन के युक्कास्यार्वी गाँव में आइसहोटल हर सर्दी तोर्ने नदी की बर्फ़ से नए सिरे से बनता है। कलाकार हर साल नए कमरे डिज़ाइन करते हैं, जिनमें बर्फ़ के पलंगों पर रेनडियर की खालें बिछी होती हैं। अंदर का तापमान लगभग शून्य से 5 डिग्री नीचे रहता है। मेहमान गर्म स्लीपिंग बैग में सोते हैं। हर बसंत कमरे पिघलकर नदी में लौट जाते हैं।

अमेरिका में हर सर्दी [[@alaska|अलास्का]] के फ़ेयरबैंक्स में वर्ल्ड आइस आर्ट चैंपियनशिप होती है। वहाँ की बर्फ़ इतनी साफ़ है कि मूर्तिकार उसे "आर्कटिक हीरा" कहते हैं।

भारत में बहुत-सी शादियों और होटलों के बुफ़े में हंस, हाथी या नामों की बर्फ़ की मूर्तियाँ सजती हैं। भारत की गर्मी में ये बस कुछ घंटे टिकती हैं, इसलिए कारीगर अक्सर उसी दिन ठंडे कमरों में इन्हें बनाते हैं और टपकता पानी समेटने वाली ट्रे में रखकर पहुँचाते हैं।

सर्दियों में [[@kashmir|कश्मीर]] में असली बर्फ़ और बर्फ़ की कला दिखती है। गुलमर्ग में दबाई हुई बर्फ़ से बना एक इग्लू कैफ़े भीड़ खींचता रहा है, जिसके अंदर मेज़ें और कुर्सियाँ भी बर्फ़ की बनी हैं।

पानी अजीब है। ज़्यादातर चीज़ें जमने पर सिकुड़ती हैं, पर पानी लगभग 9% फैल जाता है। इसीलिए फ़्रीज़र में रखी भरी काँच की बोतल चटक सकती है, और इसीलिए [[@why-ice-floats|बर्फ़ पानी पर तैरती]] है। मूर्तिकारों को यह ध्यान रखना पड़ता है, क्योंकि बहुत जल्दी गर्म या ठंडी होने पर बर्फ़ चटक सकती है।

कारीगर सिल्ली को पढ़ना भी सीखते हैं। बर्फ़ [[crystal|क्रिस्टलों]] से बनी होती है, और गलत जगह पर एक तेज़ चोट सिल्ली को किसी छिपी कमज़ोर लकीर के साथ चीर सकती है, कुछ वैसे ही जैसे लकड़ी अपने रेशों के साथ फटती है। तराशे गए हंस में दौड़ता छह-कोनों वाला वही क्रिस्टल पैटर्न हर [[@snowflake-six|हिमकण]] को भी आकार देता है, इसीलिए हिमकणों की लगभग हमेशा छह भुजाएँ होती हैं।

text: An angle measures how much something turns. A full turn is 360 degrees, so a straight line, which is half a turn, is 180 degrees.

Here is the trick. Take any triangle and draw a line through its top corner that runs [[parallel|parallel]] to the bottom edge. The three angles at the top now sit side by side along that straight line. Two of them are copies of the bottom two corners, because a line crossing two parallel lines makes matching angles. So the three corners of the triangle together make a straight line: 180 degrees.
It works for every triangle on a flat surface, fat or thin, tiny or huge.

The tiny one

st.reveal: Making a triangle bigger makes its sides longer, but its corners don't get any wider. On a flat surface, every triangle's angles add up to exactly 180 degrees, whatever its size.

myth: A bigger triangle has bigger angles that add up to more than 180 degrees.
The size of a triangle has nothing to do with its angles. A triangle drawn on a stamp and one drawn across a cricket ground can have exactly the same corners.

sec.t:
About 2,300 years ago, a Greek teacher in Alexandria named [[@euclid|Euclid]] collected the [[geometry|geometry]] of his time into a set of books called the *Elements*. Proposition 32 of the first book proves the triangle rule using the parallel-line trick above.

What made Euclid special was his method. He started with a few simple statements everyone agreed on, then built every new fact from the ones before, step by step. The *Elements* was copied, translated and taught for more than 2,000 years. It reached India, the Arab world and Europe, and parts of it are still in school textbooks today.

Euclid was not the only one working with triangles. In India, the *Sulba Sutras* were rules for building fire altars, written down well over 2,000 years ago. They already used the geometry of right-angled triangles to lay out exact shapes with ropes and pegs.

Nobody knows for sure why a full turn is 360. The idea comes from ancient Babylon, in what is now Iraq. Babylonian [[astronomer|astronomers]] [[@clocks-maths|counted in sixties]], and 360 is six sixties. It is also close to the number of days in a year, so the Sun moves about one degree a day against the stars.

The number is handy too. It divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 12, which makes it easy to split a circle into equal slices.

The 180-degree rule only works on a flat surface. On a [[@what-if-earth-flat|curved one]], things change.

Start at the North Pole and walk straight down to the [[equator|equator]]. Turn left by 90 degrees and walk a quarter of the way around the Earth. Turn left by 90 degrees again and walk back to the Pole. You have made a triangle, and every corner is a right angle. The angles add up to 270 degrees.

The bigger a triangle on a ball, the more its angles add up to. A triangle chalked on a school playground is so nearly flat that the extra is far too tiny to measure.

{{story:maps-flat}}

This is why pilots and ship captains use special maths for long journeys. It is also why no [[@maps-flat|flat map]] of the round Earth can get every shape and distance right.

Once you know the rule, you can use it. If two corners of a triangle are 60 and 70 degrees, the third must be 50. Builders and surveyors have used this for thousands of years to work out angles they can't easily measure.

Triangles are also the strongest simple shape. Push on a square frame and it squashes into a diamond. Push on a triangle and it holds, because its three sides lock the angles in place. That is why railway [[@bridges|bridges]], electricity towers and bicycle frames are full of them.

The rule also tells you about other shapes. Any flat shape with straight sides can be cut into triangles from one corner. A square makes two triangles, so its angles add to 360 degrees. A pentagon makes three, so its angles add to 540.

text: The [[@paralympics|Paralympics]] are the top sporting event for athletes with disabilities. They are held soon after the Olympics, in the same city. India has sent athletes since 1968, and in recent years Indian para-athletes have become some of the country's biggest sporting stars.

At the Tokyo 2020 Games, held in 2021, India won 19 medals. At Paris 2024, it won 29, including 7 golds, its best ever. Javelin throwers, shooters, archers, high jumpers and table tennis players have stood on the podium. Several of them faced injury, illness or poverty before they ever reached a stadium.

sec.h: A soldier who swam into history
sec.t:
Murlikant Petkar was a soldier and boxer in the Indian Army. During the 1965 war he was shot several times and badly injured. Doctors suggested swimming to help him recover.

In 1972, at the Heidelberg Paralympics in Germany, he swam the 50-metre freestyle in a world-record 37.33 seconds. It was India's first Paralympic gold. For years, few people in India knew. He was given the Padma Shri in 2018, and in 2024 a Hindi film told his story.

In 2016, Deepa Malik won silver in the shot put at Rio. She became the first Indian woman to win a Paralympic medal. She competed from a wheelchair after an illness affected her spine.

At Tokyo, the shooter Avani Lekhara won gold in the 10-metre air rifle. She was 19, and had been in a wheelchair since a car accident at age 11. In Paris in 2024, she won gold again. She became the first Indian woman to win two Paralympic golds.

sec.h: An archer who shoots with her feet
sec.t:
Sheetal Devi was born without arms in a village in Jammu and Kashmir. She learned [[@archery|archery]] by sitting on a chair, holding the bow with her right foot and pulling the string with her shoulder and jaw. Coaches built her a special technique from scratch.

At Paris 2024, aged 17, she and Rakesh Kumar won bronze in the mixed team compound event. Videos of her shooting were watched by millions around the world.

In Rio, Mariyappan Thangavelu, from a village in Tamil Nadu, won high jump gold. As a child, a bus accident had left his right leg badly damaged. He went on to win more medals at Tokyo and Paris.

Paralympic athletes compete in classes, so people with similar impairments face each other. That is why event names include codes like F64 or SH1. Each class keeps the contest fair. Other Indians have made history too. At Tokyo, Bhavina Patel won silver, India's first Paralympic medal in table tennis. At Paris, Harvinder Singh won India's first Paralympic gold in archery.

In 1948, a doctor named Ludwig Guttmann organised an archery contest for injured soldiers at Stoke Mandeville hospital in England. It grew into the first Paralympic Games, in Rome in 1960. And the strangest part? Many of the tools that help Paralympians, from racing wheelchairs to bionic hands, are now changing everyday life too, as the story of [[@accessibility-tech|accessibility technology]] shows.

text: तुम्हारा शरीर लगभग 37°C पर सबसे अच्छा काम करता है। कोशिकाओं के भीतर होने वाली रासायनिक क्रियाएँ, जिन्हें [[enzyme|एंज़ाइम]] चलाते हैं, इसी तापमान के हिसाब से ढली हैं, और अगर यह बहुत बदल जाए, तो वे ठीक से काम करना बंद कर देती हैं।

sec.t:
तुम हर समय गर्मी बना रहे होते हो। हर कोशिका [[energy|ऊर्जा]] के लिए खाना जलाती है, और उस ऊर्जा का कुछ हिस्सा गर्माहट बनकर निकलता है। चुपचाप बैठा एक बड़ा भी लगभग 100 वॉट के बल्ब जितनी गर्मी छोड़ता है। दौड़ते या खेलते समय मांसपेशियाँ इससे कहीं ज़्यादा बनाती हैं।

इसीलिए भरी हुई कक्षा इतनी जल्दी गर्म हो जाती है, और क्रिकेट मैच के बाद खिलाड़ियों के बदन से गर्म हवा उठती महसूस होती है। मुश्किल गर्मी बनाना नहीं है। मुश्किल है फ़ालतू गर्मी से छुटकारा पाना।

[[@body-cold-swimmers|जब तुम्हें ठंड लगती है]], तो त्वचा की खून की नलियाँ सिकुड़ जाती हैं, ताकि गर्म खून शरीर के भीतर गहराई में रहे। उँगलियाँ और पैर की उँगलियाँ पीली और ठंडी पड़ सकती हैं। इससे दिल, दिमाग और दूसरे [[organ|अंग]] सुरक्षित रहते हैं।

अगर इतना काफ़ी न हो, तो तुम काँपने लगते हो। काँपना असल में मांसपेशियों का बहुत तेज़ी से कसना और ढीला होना है, जिससे गर्मी बनती है। रोंगटे खड़े होना हमारे रोएँदार पूर्वजों से मिली निशानी है। घने बालों वाले जानवरों में बाल खड़े करने से गर्म हवा की एक परत फँस जाती है। इंसानों के शरीर पर बाल कम हैं, इसलिए इससे ज़्यादा फ़ायदा नहीं होता।

किसी [[infection|संक्रमण]] के दौरान रोग-प्रतिरोधक तंत्र हाइपोथैलेमस से अपनी सेटिंग बढ़ाने को कहता है। यही [[@fever|बुखार]] है। तापमान चढ़ते हुए भी तुम्हें ठंड लग सकती है और कँपकँपी छूट सकती है, क्योंकि शरीर नई, ऊँची सेटिंग तक पहुँचने की कोशिश कर रहा होता है। बहुत-से वैज्ञानिक मानते हैं कि बुखार शरीर को कीटाणुओं से लड़ने में मदद करता है।

बाहर की बहुत ज़्यादा गर्मी इस पूरे तंत्र पर भारी पड़ सकती है। भारत और अमेरिका में तेज़ [[@heatwaves|लू]] के दौरान बाहर काम करने वाले लोग, बुज़ुर्ग और नन्हे बच्चे लू लगने के सबसे ज़्यादा खतरे में होते हैं, जब शरीर का तापमान खतरनाक हद तक चढ़ जाता है। पानी पीना, छाँव में आराम करना और सबसे गर्म घंटों से बचना, सब मदद करते हैं। गर्मी में अगर किसी को चक्कर आए, उलझन हो या पसीना आना बंद हो जाए, तो उसे फ़ौरन किसी बड़े की मदद चाहिए।

1868 में जर्मन डॉक्टर कार्ल वुंडरलिक ने हज़ारों मरीज़ों के शरीर के तापमान छापे और 37°C को सामान्य माना। फ़ारेनहाइट में बदलने पर यह 98.6°F बन गया। 2020 में अमेरिका की स्टैनफ़र्ड यूनिवर्सिटी के शोधकर्ताओं ने पुराने और नए रिकॉर्डों की तुलना की और पाया कि 1800 के दशक के बाद से औसत अमेरिकी का तापमान थोड़ा घटा है। उनका अनुमान है कि इसकी वजह कम बीमारियाँ और ज़्यादा आरामदेह घर हो सकते हैं। डॉक्टर अब 37°C को कोई पक्का नियम नहीं, बल्कि एक काम का औसत मानते हैं, क्योंकि सेहतमंद लोग भी एक-दूसरे से थोड़े अलग होते हैं।

text: अकेलापन वह उदास, ख़ाली-ख़ाली एहसास है जो तब होता है जब दूसरों के साथ तुम्हारी नज़दीकी तुम्हारी ज़रूरत से कम हो। हो सकता है लंच में साथ बैठने के लिए कोई न हो। हो सकता है तुम ऐसे लोगों से घिरे हो जो तुम्हें समझते ही न हों।

यह अकेले होने से अलग है। किसी शांत दोपहर में अकेले बैठकर किताब पढ़ना बहुत प्यारा लग सकता है। इसे अक्सर एकांत कहते हैं। अकेलापन तब है जब अकेले होना चुभने लगे। लगभग हर किसी को कभी न कभी ऐसा लगता है, घर बदलने के बाद, स्कूल बदलने पर, किसी दोस्त के दूर हो जाने पर, या बस किसी बुरे हफ़्ते में। आम तौर पर यह गुज़र जाता है। अगर यह लंबे समय तक बना रहे, तो किसी से बात करना अच्छा रहता है।

sec.t:
बहुत-से वैज्ञानिक मानते हैं कि अकेलापन भूख या प्यास की तरह काम करता है। भूख जान-बूझकर बुरी लगती है: वह तुम्हें खाना ढूँढने को धकेलती है। अकेलापन शायद तुम्हें लोगों को ढूँढने के लिए धकेलता है।

हमारे शुरुआती [[ancestor|पूर्वजों]] के लिए किसी समूह का हिस्सा होने का मतलब था सुरक्षा, बँटा हुआ खाना, और चोट लगने पर मदद। जो अकेला छूट जाता, वह ख़तरे में होता। तो जिस दिमाग को दूसरों से कटकर बुरा लगता, उसके पास संगत ढूँढने की एक वजह थी। इससे समझ आता है कि अकेलापन लगभग शरीर के दर्द जैसा, एक टीस जैसा क्यों लग सकता है। लोग जिन [[@emotions|भावनाओं]] की बात करते हैं, उनमें यह सबसे गहरी भावनाओं में से एक है।

शोधकर्ता यह भी कहते हैं कि अकेलेपन में गिनती से ज़्यादा रिश्तों की गहराई मायने रखती है। एक पक्का दोस्त, जिससे तुम दिल खोलकर बात कर सको, शायद उस बड़े ग्रुप से बेहतर बचाता है जिसका तुम कभी हिस्सा महसूस नहीं करते।

sec.h: युवा भी इसे क्यों महसूस करते हैं
sec.t:
सुनने में अजीब लग सकता है, पर किशोर और युवा ज़्यादातर बुज़ुर्गों से ज़्यादा अकेलेपन की बात कहते हैं। बड़े होने में बहुत कुछ बदलता है। दोस्तों के ग्रुप बदल जाते हैं। लोग पढ़ाई या नौकरी के लिए दूर चले जाते हैं। ख़ुद को सबसे अलग महसूस करना, या ऑनलाइन किसी ग्रुप से बाहर कर दिया जाना, चुभ सकता है।

फ़ोन ने मामला और उलझा दिया है। मैसेज से पुणे वाले चचेरे भाई या टेक्सस चले गए दोस्त से नज़दीकी बनी रह सकती है। पर दूसरों की पार्टियों की तस्वीरें स्क्रॉल करते-करते अपनी शाम और सूनी लग सकती है। शोधकर्ता अब भी बहस करते हैं कि [[@screen-time|स्क्रीन]] अकेलेपन को कितना बढ़ाती हैं और कितना घटाती हैं।

छोटे कदम भी गिने जाते हैं। थोड़ी-सी गपशप, कोई साझा मज़ाक, या दूसरों के साथ कोई काम, जैसे कोई टीम, क्लब या गाने का ग्रुप, बिना ज़्यादा दबाव के जुड़ाव बनाते हैं। किसी और की मदद करने से अक्सर मदद करने वाले का भी भला होता है, कुछ इसलिए कि इससे बात करने का बहाना मिल जाता है।

दूसरों का अकेलापन पहचानना भी ज़रूरी है। क्लास में आया नया बच्चा, अकेले रहने वाले दादा-दादी, कोई दोस्त जो अचानक चुप-चुप रहने लगा हो: कुछ मिनट की [[@empathy|हमदर्दी]] उनका दिन बदल सकती है। सच्ची [[@friendship|दोस्ती]] आम तौर पर छोटी-सी शुरुआत से ही बनती है।

कुछ जगहें नए तरीके आज़मा रही हैं। ब्रिटेन में डॉक्टर बागवानी क्लब, गाने के ग्रुप या साथ टहलने वाले ग्रुप जैसी गतिविधियाँ "दवा की पर्ची" पर लिख सकते हैं। इस तरीके को सोशल प्रिस्क्राइबिंग कहते हैं। कुछ स्कूलों के मैदान में एक "दोस्ती की बेंच" होती है। जिस बच्चे को साथी चाहिए, वह वहाँ बैठ जाता है, और बाकी बच्चे जानते हैं कि उसे खेलने बुलाना है।

अगर तुम्हें लंबे समय तक अकेलापन लगे, या मन बहुत उदास रहे, तो किसी भरोसेमंद बड़े को बताओ, जैसे माता-पिता, टीचर या स्कूल काउंसलर। वे मदद कर सकते हैं। और यह बात ज़ोर से कह देना अक्सर सबसे मुश्किल, पर सबसे काम का कदम होता है।

text: ज़ुकाम में तुम्हारी जीभ तब भी काम करती है। काम करना बंद करती है सूँघने की ताकत, और खाने का ज़्यादातर ज़ायका गंध से ही आता है।

जीभ सिर्फ़ कुछ गिने-चुने बुनियादी स्वाद पहचान सकती है: मीठा, नमकीन, खट्टा, कड़वा और [[@food-science-umami|उमामी]], जो एक चटपटा-सा, नमकीन ज़ायका है। बाकी सब, जैसे आम और केले का फ़र्क या बिरयानी की महक, गंध से आता है। चबाते समय खुशबू के [[molecule|अणु]] मुँह के पिछले हिस्से से ऊपर तैरकर नाक में पहुँचते हैं। ज़ुकाम सूजे हुए ऊतक और [[mucus|बलगम]] से यह रास्ता बंद कर देता है, इसलिए खाना फीका लगता है।

sec.t:
गंध नाक तक दो रास्तों से पहुँचती है। फूल सूँघते समय खुशबू नथुनों से अंदर जाती है। खाते समय गंध पिछले रास्ते से जाती है, मुँह से गले होते हुए ऊपर नाक में। वैज्ञानिक इसे रेट्रोनेज़ल गंध कहते हैं, यानी पीछे के रास्ते वाली गंध।

तुम्हारा दिमाग़ पिछले दरवाज़े से आई इस गंध को जीभ के संकेतों के साथ मिला देता है, और तुम्हें एक ही चीज़ महसूस होती है: ज़ायका। लगता है कि सब कुछ मुँह में हो रहा है। इसीलिए ज़्यादातर लोग यह जानकर हैरान होते हैं कि उनकी [[@nose-smell|नाक]] कितना काम कर रही है।

sec.h: ज़ुकाम इसे बंद क्यों कर देता है
sec.t:
हर नथुने के बिल्कुल ऊपर डाक टिकट जितना ऊतक का एक टुकड़ा होता है। इसमें गंध भाँपने वाली लाखों कोशिकाएँ हैं, जिनमें लगभग 400 तरह के [[receptor|रिसेप्टर]] होते हैं। पहचाने जाने के लिए गंध के अणुओं को इस टुकड़े तक पहुँचना और इसकी नम परत में घुलना पड़ता है।

[[@cold-flu|ज़ुकाम]] में नाक का अंदरूनी हिस्सा सूज जाता है और बलगम से भर जाता है। हवा, और उसमें घुली गंध, गंध वाले टुकड़े तक नहीं पहुँच पाती। सूजन उतरने पर ज़ायका आमतौर पर कुछ दिनों में लौट आता है। कुछ वायरस, जिनमें कोविड-19 वाला वायरस भी है, गंध पर ज़्यादा सीधा और लंबा असर डाल सकते हैं।

हरी मिर्च या तीखी सब्ज़ी की जलन कोई स्वाद है ही नहीं। यह [[capsaicin|कैप्साइसिन]] नाम के एक रसायन से आती है, जो वही [[nerve|नसें]] जगा देता है जो गरमी और दर्द भाँपती हैं। इसीलिए [[@spicy-hot|तीखा खाना]] खाकर पसीना आ सकता है और आँखों से पानी बह सकता है, और इसीलिए मिर्च काटने के बाद आँख छू लो तो जलन होती है।

पुदीने की ठंडक इसी तरह, बस उल्टे ढंग से काम करती है। मेंथॉल ठंडक भाँपने वाली नसें जगा देता है, जबकि पुदीना असल में ठंडा नहीं होता।

sec.h: वह इंद्रिय, जो जाने पर याद आती है
sec.t:
ज़्यादातर लोग गंध के बारे में तब तक नहीं सोचते जब तक वह चली न जाए। जो लोग लंबे समय तक सूँघने की ताकत खो देते हैं, जिसे एनॉस्मिया कहते हैं, वे अक्सर बताते हैं कि खाना बेरंग हो गया, और धुएँ या फटे दूध जैसे चेतावनी के संकेत भी छूट जाते हैं।

नाक तुम्हारी यादों को भी गढ़ती है। किसी ख़ास खाने की एक महक पल भर में कोई छुट्टी या नानी-दादी की रसोई याद दिला सकती है। गंध के संकेत दूसरी इंद्रियों के मुकाबले ज़्यादा सीधे दिमाग़ के उन हिस्सों तक पहुँचते हैं जो भावनाओं और यादों से जुड़े हैं।

text: विज्ञान कहता है कि योग कसरत का एक अच्छा तरीका है जो कुछ ख़ास दिक्कतों में मदद कर सकता है, पर यह हर मर्ज़ की दवा नहीं। सावधानी से किए गए अध्ययन दिखाते हैं कि इससे लचीलापन, संतुलन और ताकत बढ़ सकती है। यह लंबे समय के कमर दर्द में लगभग उतनी ही राहत दे सकता है जितनी दूसरी कसरत। बहुत-से लोग कहते हैं कि इससे [[@stress|तनाव]] घटता है और नींद अच्छी आती है, और कुछ अध्ययन भी यही कहते हैं, हालाँकि असर आमतौर पर हल्का होता है।

बड़े दावों, जैसे योग से डायबिटीज़, दिल की बीमारी या कैंसर ठीक होना, के पीछे कोई पक्का सबूत नहीं है। इसका मतलब यह नहीं कि योग बेकार है। मतलब यह है कि इसके फ़ायदे असली हैं, पर कुछ विज्ञापनों के दावों से कहीं ज़्यादा साधारण।

योग को परखना आसान नहीं। जैसे किसी को नकली गोली दी जा सकती है, वैसे नकली योग नहीं कराया जा सकता, इसलिए लोगों को पता होता है कि वे योग कर रहे हैं। बहुत-से अध्ययन छोटे और थोड़े समय के होते हैं। शोधकर्ता योग की तुलना दूसरी कसरतों से करने की कोशिश करते हैं, ताकि देख सकें कि यह कुछ ख़ास करता है या नहीं।

सबसे अच्छे नतीजे लंबे समय के कमर दर्द, संतुलन और लचीलेपन के लिए हैं। दूसरी देखभाल के साथ-साथ योग कुछ लोगों को हल्की घबराहट और उदासी में भी मदद करता लगता है। धीमी साँस कुछ देर के लिए दिल की धड़कन शांत कर सकती है, जिससे शायद समझ आता है कि सत्र के बाद लोग हल्का क्यों महसूस करते हैं। कुछ फ़ायदे बस हिलने-डुलने, आराम करने और बेहतर महसूस करने की उम्मीद से भी आ सकते हैं, जो कुछ हद तक [[@placebo|प्लेसिबो]] असर है।

भारत और दूसरी जगहों के वैज्ञानिक प्राणायाम, यानी योग के साँस वाले अभ्यासों, का भी अध्ययन करते हैं। धीमी, गहरी साँस थोड़ी देर के लिए दिल की धड़कन और ब्लड [[pressure|प्रेशर]] कम कर सकती है। बरसों के अभ्यास से टिकाऊ फ़ायदे मिलते हैं या नहीं, इसे अभी बड़े परीक्षणों में परखा जा रहा है। 2014 में बना भारत का आयुष मंत्रालय इस शोध के कुछ हिस्से के लिए पैसा देता है।

योग की बहुत-सी कक्षाएँ शांत साँस या चुपचाप लेटने के साथ ख़त्म होती हैं। यह हिस्सा [[@mindfulness|माइंडफ़ुलनेस]] के क़रीब है, जो ध्यान को इसी पल पर टिकाए रखना सिखाती है। अध्ययन बताते हैं कि माइंडफ़ुलनेस बहुत-से लोगों का तनाव थोड़ा कम कर सकती है।

योग शरीर के प्रति सजगता भी सिखाता है। किसी आसन में टिके रहने से तुम ध्यान देते हो कि कैसे खड़े होते हो, बैठते हो और साँस लेते हो। इससे [[@posture|बैठने-खड़े होने के ढंग]] में मदद मिल सकती है, हालाँकि झुककर बैठना उतना ख़तरनाक नहीं जितना कभी-कभी बताया जाता है।

भारत के प्रस्ताव के बाद 2014 में संयुक्त राष्ट्र ने 21 जून को अंतरराष्ट्रीय योग दिवस घोषित किया। यह उत्तरी [[hemisphere|गोलार्ध]] में साल का सबसे लंबा दिन है। 2016 में यूनेस्को ने योग को दुनिया की जीवित सांस्कृतिक धरोहर की सूची में जोड़ा। 2015 में पहले अंतरराष्ट्रीय योग दिवस पर नई दिल्ली के राजपथ पर लगभग 36,000 लोगों ने एक साथ योग किया, जिससे सबसे बड़ी योग कक्षा का गिनीज़ विश्व रिकॉर्ड बना।

योग ज़्यादातर लोगों के लिए सुरक्षित है, पर आसनों में बहुत ज़ोर लगाने से चोट लग सकती है, ख़ासकर मरोड़ वाले आसनों और शीर्षासन में। प्रशिक्षित शिक्षक मदद करता है, ख़ासकर शुरुआत करने वालों की, जो अक्सर शरीर के तैयार होने से पहले ही ऑनलाइन देखे आसनों की नकल करने लगते हैं। जिन्हें कोई बीमारी है, उन्हें पहले डॉक्टर से पूछना चाहिए। आराम से किया जाए, तो यह शरीर को चलता-फिरता रखने का एक और तरीका है, चाहे पुणे के किसी पार्क में हो या अमेरिका के पोर्टलैंड के किसी जिम में।

text: [[encryption|Encryption]] turns a readable message into scrambled nonsense, so only someone with the right key can turn it back. The scrambling follows a set of maths rules. The key is a secret number that tells the rules exactly how to scramble and unscramble.

Your phone uses encryption all the time: when you send a chat message, pay with a phone, or visit a website with a padlock in the address bar. Anyone who intercepts the data along the way sees only gibberish. Without the key, breaking modern encryption by guessing would take today's computers far longer than the universe has existed.

st.prompt: In a Caesar cipher each letter shifts three places along the alphabet, so A becomes D. What does the code word FDW mean?

options.t: CAT
DOG
HAT

st.reveal: Shift each letter back three places. F goes to C, D goes to A, and W goes to T. With only 25 possible shifts, anyone can crack a Caesar cipher in minutes, which is why modern codes use vastly more possibilities.

Strong encryption is extremely hard to break, but weak keys, stolen passwords or mistakes in software can let people in. Codes also age, as computers get faster, so experts keep replacing old methods with stronger ones.

sec.t:
People have hidden messages for thousands of years. Julius Caesar is said to have used a simple [[cipher|cipher]]: move every letter three places along [[@words-alphabet-order|the alphabet]], so A becomes D and B becomes E. "CAT" becomes "FDW".

The weakness is that there are only 25 possible shifts. An enemy can try them all in minutes. Even trickier ciphers can be cracked by counting letters, since E is the most common letter in English. The Arab scholar al-Kindi described this trick in the 800s, and it has cracked many of history's [[@cipher-codes|secret codes]] since.

Old ciphers had one big problem. Both people needed the same secret key, and handing it over safely was hard. In 1976, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published a way around it, and soon after, a method called RSA put the idea to work.

It works like an open padlock. You hand out copies of your padlock to anyone. They can snap it shut on a box with a message inside. But only you have the key that opens it. In computers, the "padlock" is a public key and the "key" is a private one, linked by maths involving huge [[@prime-numbers|prime numbers]].

Modern methods such as AES use keys with 128 or 256 [[@binary-code|binary]] digits. A 128-bit key has about 340 followed by 36 zeros possible values. A computer testing a billion billion keys every second would need over ten trillion years to try them all. That is hundreds of times the age of the universe.

So attackers rarely try. Instead they steal [[@passwords|passwords]], trick people, or look for mistakes in software.

Many messaging apps now use end-to-end encryption, which means even the company running the app cannot read your messages. Supporters say this protects ordinary people, journalists and businesses. Some police and governments worry it also hides criminals, and want a way to read messages with a court's permission. Security experts warn that any secret back door could be found by others too. The debate continues around the world.

Looking ahead, powerful quantum computers might one day break some of today's public-key methods. In 2024 the US standards agency NIST published new methods designed to resist them.

text: Sort of, but not like in films. Scientists have made "cloaks" that bend waves around small objects so that they seem to vanish. The first, built at Duke University in North Carolina in 2006, hid a small copper cylinder from microwaves, the kind of waves used for radar and wifi.

Hiding something from visible light, the light our eyes see, is much harder. Visible light has very short waves and many colours. The cloaks that work for it so far are small, work only from some angles, or use simple tricks with lenses and mirrors. A coat that makes you vanish from every direction is still science fiction.

st.prompt: Why would a perfectly invisible person not be able to see anything?

options.t: Because eyes must absorb light to see, and absorbing light would make them visible
Because invisibility would make them fall asleep
Because their eyes would be too far apart

st.reveal: Seeing works when light hits the retina and is absorbed. If light passed straight through a person, it would pass through their eyes too, and they would see nothing. Even an invisible person's eyes would show up as two dark dots.

src: Schurig D., Pendry J. B., Smith D. R. et al. (2006), Metamaterial electromagnetic cloak at microwave frequencies, Science.
Ou Z. et al. (2024), Achieving optical transparency in live animals with absorbing molecules, Science.
n.certNote: Small invisibility cloaks that work for some kinds of waves, or from certain angles, are real. A cloak that hides a person from every angle in ordinary light is far beyond today's technology, and some physicists doubt it is possible.

Real cloaks hide small objects, from certain angles, or for certain kinds of waves such as microwaves. Some cheap lens tricks can hide things from one viewpoint. Nobody has made a flexible cloak that hides a person in ordinary light from every direction.

sec.t:
In 2006, physicists led by John Pendry in London and David Smith at Duke designed a ring of special materials called metamaterials. These are made of tiny repeating structures, smaller than the waves they control, that can steer waves in unusual directions. The ring guided microwaves around the object inside, like water flowing round a rock and joining up again behind it.

Since then, researchers have made cloaks that hide small objects from visible light, using crystals or tiny patterned surfaces, but usually only for one colour or from one direction. Making a large, flexible metamaterial for every colour is the big unsolved challenge.

In 2014, scientists at the University of Rochester used four ordinary lenses to make a simple cloak that hid objects behind it from a range of viewpoints. Other inventors use "lenticular" sheets, the ridged plastic found on some 3D postcards, which can blur out an object standing behind them.

These cloaks work best if you stand in the right place. They are fun, but you can usually see that something odd is going on.

Nature had the idea first. Glass frogs in Central and South American rainforests have see-through bellies, and when they sleep they hide most of their red blood cells in their liver to become even harder to see. Many [[@jellyfish-old|jellyfish]], shrimp and baby eels in the sea are almost transparent.

In 2024, scientists at Stanford University found a surprising way to make living skin transparent. They rubbed tartrazine, a yellow dye used in snacks and drinks, onto the bellies of mice. It made the skin bend light more evenly, so the scientists could see organs underneath. When the dye was washed off, the skin went back to normal. The method could help doctors look under the skin without cutting.

Some of the most useful invisibility has nothing to do with eyes. Stealth aircraft are shaped with flat angles and coated in special materials so that [[@radio-waves|radio waves]] from radar bounce away instead of back to the radar station. To radar, a large plane can look as small as a bird.

There is a strange catch for anyone hoping to become invisible. Your eyes work by absorbing light. A perfectly invisible person would let light pass through their eyes, so they would see nothing at all. A real invisible spy would need two little dark dots for eyes.

Animals have found a cleverer answer than vanishing. They blend in instead, and some of the best at it are explained in [[@camouflage|camouflage]].

text: Quite a few. Penicillin, the first widely used [[@antibiotics|antibiotic]], was found when mould landed on a dish of [[bacteria|bacteria]]. X-rays were discovered when a screen glowed unexpectedly. The microwave oven, Post-it Notes, [[@non-stick-pans|Teflon non-stick pans]] and [[@accident-superglue|superglue]] all began with mistakes or surprises.

But "accident" is only half the story. In every case, someone noticed that something strange had happened, wondered why, and then did years of careful work. The French scientist Louis Pasteur put it well in 1854: in the field of observation, chance favours only the prepared mind.

st.prompt: In 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen noticed something odd while testing a glass tube in a darkened room. What was it?

options.t: A screen across the room started to glow
The tube started to play music
His pencil floated in the air

st.reveal: Even with the tube covered in black card, a chemical-coated screen nearby glowed. Invisible rays were escaping and passing through the card. He called them X-rays because X stands for something unknown.

n.certNote: The main facts about these discoveries are well recorded, but some famous details, such as exactly what was in Percy Spencer's pocket, have been retold so often that they may have changed along the way.

sec.t:
In November 1895, the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen was testing a glass tube that gave off electrical rays. He had covered it with black card, yet a chemical-coated screen across the dark room began to glow. Something invisible was passing through the card.

He soon found the rays went through paper, wood and even flesh, but not bone or metal. One of his first [[@x-rays|X-ray]] pictures showed the bones of his wife's hand, with her ring. Within months, doctors around the world were using X-rays to find broken bones and swallowed coins.

In 1945 an American engineer, Percy Spencer, was working near a magnetron, a device that makes radio waves for radar. He noticed that a [[@chocolate-tree|chocolate]] bar in his pocket had melted. Curious, he tried [[@popcorn|popcorn]] kernels, which popped, and then an egg, which exploded.

Spencer's company built the first [[@microwave|microwave oven]] in 1947. It was nearly as tall as a fridge and cost thousands of dollars. Smaller ovens for homes became common in the 1970s and 1980s.

In 1968 Spencer Silver, a scientist at the company 3M, was trying to make a very strong [[@glue-sticky|glue]]. Instead, he made a weak one that stuck lightly and peeled off cleanly. Nobody knew what to do with it.

Years later, his colleague Art Fry was annoyed that his paper bookmarks kept falling out of his church hymn book. He used Silver's glue to make bookmarks that stayed put but didn't tear the pages. Post-it Notes went on sale in 1980.

Some inventions come from noticing nature. In 1941 the [[@switzerland|Swiss engineer]] George de Mestral went walking with his dog and found burrs stuck in its fur. Under a [[microscope|microscope]], he saw tiny hooks catching on loops. That gave him the idea for [[@velcro|Velcro]], though it took him years to make it work.

A favourite story says an 11-year-old in California, Frank Epperson, left a fruit drink with a stirring stick outside on a cold night in 1905 and found it frozen solid. He later sold the idea as the Popsicle, a cousin of the [[@ice-cream|ice cream]] on a stick. Like many inventors, he then protected it with a [[@patents|patent]], granted in 1924.

text: A jet engine pulls air in at the front, squeezes it, burns fuel in it, and blasts it out of the back. Engineers sum it up as "suck, squeeze, bang, blow".

The hot gas rushing backwards pushes the engine, and the plane, forwards. This follows a rule described by Isaac [[@newton-life|Newton]]: every push has an equal push in the opposite direction. On the way out, the hot gas also spins a set of blades called a [[turbine|turbine]], which drives the compressor at the front. So the engine keeps itself running for as long as it has fuel.

st.prompt: In a modern airliner engine, where does most of the air that comes in go?

options.t: Around the outside of the engine core, pushed by the big fan
Into the fire in the middle of the engine
Out through the windows of the plane for passengers to breathe

st.reveal: In the turbofan engines on most airliners, the giant front fan pushes most of the air around the core rather than through it. This big, slower stream of air gives most of the push, and it is quieter and uses less fuel than blasting a small stream out very fast.

src: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Propulsion.
Science Museum Group (London), Whittle W.1 jet engine.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, jet engine.

myth: A jet engine moves the plane by pushing against the air behind it.

The engine throws a huge amount of air backwards very fast, and the air pushes back on the engine, driving it forward. It doesn't need anything behind it to push against. Rockets work the same way, which is why they can fly in empty space.

sec.t:
**Suck.** At the front, a large fan draws in air, up to more than a tonne of it every second at take-off in the biggest engines.

**Squeeze.** The air passes through a compressor, rows of small spinning blades that squash it tighter and tighter. Squeezed air gets hot, the way a bicycle pump warms up.

**Bang.** In the [[combustion|combustion]] chamber, fuel is sprayed into the squeezed air and [[@fire-burns|burns]] steadily. It isn't really a bang but a continuous roaring flame.

**Blow.** The hot gas expands and rushes out of the back. On the way, it spins the turbine, which is joined by a shaft to the compressor and fan.

The first jet engines pushed all their air through the flame and out of a narrow nozzle. They were loud and thirsty. Most airliners now use turbofans. A giant fan at the front pushes most of the air around the outside of the hot core instead.

Moving a large amount of air fairly slowly turns out to be more efficient than moving a little air very fast. On the biggest engines, the fan is about 3.4 metres across. Most of the push comes from this cool stream of air, which is also quieter.

sec.h: Hotter than the metal can stand

sec.t:
In 1930, Frank Whittle, a young officer in Britain's Royal Air Force, patented a design for a jet engine. Few people were interested, and he struggled for money for years. Meanwhile, in [[@germany|Germany]], Hans von Ohain was working on the same idea independently. His engine powered the first jet aeroplane flight on 27 August 1939, just days before the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]] began in Europe. Whittle's engine flew in 1941.

After the war, jets changed travel. They could fly higher, above most bad weather, and far faster than [[propeller|propeller]] planes. A trip from Mumbai to London, which once took days with many stops, now takes about ten hours.

India's air force flies jets including the Tejas, a light fighter designed in India. Its engine is American-made, but Indian scientists have spent many years developing their own jet engine, called Kaveri. [[@made-planes|Building jet engines]] is one of the hardest jobs in engineering, and only a handful of countries can make the most powerful ones.

Today, the jets that carry passengers cruise at about 900 km/h, around 10 to 12 km up, often riding fast winds called [[@jet-streams|jet streams]].

text: A search engine works in three main steps. First, programs called crawlers visit web pages, read them and follow their links to find more pages, day and night. Second, everything they find is stored in an index, a giant list of which words appear on which pages, kept on thousands of computers. Third, when you type a search, the engine looks up your words in the index and ranks the matching pages, putting the ones it thinks are most useful at the top.
All the hard work happens before you search. That's why results appear almost instantly.

st.prompt: When you type a search, what does the search engine actually look through?

options.t: Its own giant index, built in advance, like the index at the back of a book
Every website on the internet, visited at that moment
Only websites that have paid to be included

st.reveal: Searching the live web for every question would take far too long. Instead, search engines constantly visit pages ahead of time and build a huge index listing which words appear on which pages. Your search looks up that index, which is why it's so fast.

src: Google, How Search Works.
Brin S. and Page L. (1998) The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual Web search engine. Computer Networks and ISDN Systems 30.

Search engines rank pages by many signals, such as how relevant and popular they seem, but they can't check whether everything on a page is true. Some top results are adverts. It's worth checking who wrote a page and comparing several sources.

sec.t:
Crawlers, sometimes called [[@spiders-silk|spiders]], are programs that act like tireless readers. They start with a list of known pages, download them, and note every link. Then they visit those links, and the links on those pages, and so on, spreading across the [[@web-invented|web]].

They return to popular pages often, to spot changes, and to quieter ones less often. Website owners can leave instructions telling crawlers which pages to skip. Even so, crawlers can't reach everything: pages behind logins, for example, stay hidden.

Finding pages that match is only the start. A search for "tiger" might match millions of pages. Which come first?

In 1996, two students at Stanford University in California, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, had an idea. A page that many other pages link to is probably useful, especially if those linking pages are themselves important. They treated links like votes. This method, called PageRank, helped make their search engine, Google, better than its rivals when it launched in 1998.

Today's ranking uses many more signals, set by complex [[@algorithms|algorithms]]. It considers how well a page matches your words, how trustworthy the site seems, whether it works well on phones, what language you speak and roughly where you are.

The first search tool, Archie, was made in 1990 at McGill University in Canada. It searched lists of files, not web pages. In the mid-1990s, Yahoo began as a directory of websites sorted by hand, a bit like a library catalogue, and AltaVista let people search the text of millions of pages.

The name Google is a play on "[[@large-numbers-names|googol]]", 1 followed by 100 zeros, a number far bigger than the number of [[atom|atoms]] in the known universe.

Search engines are powerful, but they're not perfect judges of truth. Some results at the top are adverts, labelled as sponsored. Some websites are designed to rank highly without being reliable. And results can differ from person to person, depending on location and language.

Librarians have long taught people to ask who wrote something, when, and why. Those questions, also used in [[@libraries|libraries]], are just as useful online. Checking more than one good source is the best defence against [[@fake-news|false information]].

text: Yes, ninjas were real. In Japan they were usually called *shinobi*, which means someone who sneaks in. Between about 1450 and 1650, Japan was split into warring [[territory|territories]]. Lords hired shinobi to spy on enemies, sneak into castles, set fires, spread false rumours and gather information.

But the ninja of films, all in black, running across rooftops and throwing star-shaped blades, is mostly made up. Real shinobi were closer to spies and special soldiers than superheroes. Their best tool was blending in.

sec.t:
From the late 1400s, Japan fell into more than a century of fighting known as the Sengoku period, the "Age of Warring States". Rival lords, called daimyo, fought for land and power. They needed to know what their enemies were planning.

Two mountain areas in central Japan, Iga and Koka, became famous for shinobi. These areas were run by groups of local families rather than one big lord. They were good at guerrilla fighting and spying, and other lords hired them. In 1581, the warlord Oda Nobunaga invaded Iga with a huge army and crushed it.

sec.h: Where the black suit came from
sec.t:
In Japanese kabuki and puppet theatre, stagehands wear black from head to toe. They move props on stage, and the audience agrees to ignore them, as if they were invisible. When playwrights wanted a ninja to appear suddenly and kill someone, they had him dressed like a stagehand. The audience got the joke.

Later novels, comics and films took the costume and ran with it. By the 1960s, ninja films were popular in Japan, and by the 1980s ninjas were everywhere in America, from movies to the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.

Japan was not alone. More than 2,000 years ago, the *Arthashastra*, linked to [[@chanakya|Chanakya]], described a whole system of royal spies. They disguised themselves as students, monks, traders and holy men. They passed messages in code and reported back to the king.

[[@spies-india|Spies in India]] kept working through many kingdoms. The Mughals ran a network of news-writers across their [[empire|empire]]. Every powerful state, it seems, invents its own ninjas.

In 2017, Mie University, in the old Iga region, opened the International Ninja Research Center. Scholars there study real old ninja manuals, letters and family records. In 2018, the first student finished a master's degree there with ninja history as a focus.

In the city of Iga, there's a ninja museum with trick houses: secret doors, hidden rooms and floorboards that squeak on purpose to warn of intruders. The real ninja skill wasn't magic. It was knowing how people notice things, and how to slip past without being seen at all. Many animals do it better than any human, using [[@camouflage|camouflage]] that took millions of years to perfect.

text: Zheng He was an admiral of [[@china-today|China]]'s Ming [[dynasty|dynasty]] who led seven great voyages across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433. His fleets visited Southeast Asia, India, Sri Lanka, Arabia and East Africa.

The biggest ships, called treasure ships, were enormous. Ming records describe them as about 44 *zhang* long, roughly 120 to 135 metres, longer than a football field. Many historians doubt this, because wooden ships of that size would be very hard to build and steer. Even cautious estimates of 60 to 75 metres make them several times longer than Columbus's Santa María, which was probably about 18 metres. The fleets also carried warships, supply ships, water tankers and horse transports.

st.prompt: In 1414, ships returning from Zheng He's voyages brought an animal to the Ming court that people thought was a magical creature. Which animal?

options.t: A giraffe
A kangaroo

st.reveal: The giraffe was a gift sent from Bengal, which had received it from East Africa. At the Chinese court, people linked it with the qilin, a gentle creature of legend that was said to appear in times of good rule. Court artists painted it.
