sec.t:
Zheng He was born in 1371 in Yunnan, in southwest China, into a Muslim family. His birth name was Ma He. When Ming armies conquered Yunnan, he was captured as a boy and sent to serve in the household of a prince, Zhu Di.

He grew into a tall, capable officer and helped Zhu Di seize the throne in 1402. The new emperor, known as Yongle, gave him the name Zheng and put him in charge of a plan to show China's power across the seas.

Every one of the seven voyages stopped at Calicut, today's Kozhikode in [[@kerala|Kerala]]. It was one of the busiest ports in the Indian Ocean, a market for pepper, cotton cloth and gems.

In [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], the fleet left a stone tablet at Galle in 1409, carved in three languages: Chinese, Tamil and Persian. It records gifts to [[@buddha|the Buddha]], to a Hindu god and to Allah. It was found in 1911 and is now in the National Museum in Colombo.

The voyages were mainly about prestige and trade. Zheng He carried silk, porcelain and gold as gifts, and invited rulers to send envoys to the emperor. Dozens of kingdoms did.

Later voyages reached Hormuz in Persia, Aden in Arabia and Malindi and Mogadishu on the African coast. In 1414, a giraffe arrived at the Ming court, sent from Bengal. The court saw it as a qilin, a creature of legend that appears under a wise ruler. The fleets also fought [[@pirates|pirates]] and sometimes local armies, so they were not always peaceful.

The voyages cost a fortune. After Yongle died in 1424, many officials argued that the money was better spent at home, on defending the northern border against the Mongols.

Zheng He led one last voyage in 1431 and probably died on the way back, around 1433. China then turned away from long ocean voyages. Some records of the voyages are said to have been destroyed by officials who opposed them. Just a few decades later, Portuguese ships rounded Africa and reached Calicut themselves, in 1498.

text: Madagascar is a huge island in the Indian Ocean, off the south-east coast of Africa. It has been cut off from every other landmass for tens of millions of years. Its plants and animals have been [[evolve|evolving]] alone all that time, with no fresh arrivals walking in from outside.

The result is a land of [[species|species]] seen nowhere else. About 90 percent of its plants and animals are found only in Madagascar. It has more than a hundred kinds of lemur, about half the world's chameleons, strange spiny forests, and six kinds of baobab tree that grow wild nowhere else. Scientists sometimes call it the world's eighth continent.

st.prompt: Lemurs are primates, like monkeys, apes and us. How did their ancestors most likely reach Madagascar?

options.t: Floating across the sea from Africa on rafts of fallen trees and plants
Walking across a land bridge that later sank
They were brought by the first human settlers

st.reveal: Lemurs arrived tens of millions of years ago, long before humans. Most scientists think a few small animals were washed out to sea on tangles of vegetation after storms and survived the trip. Ocean currents at the time may have flowed towards Madagascar, making it easier.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Madagascar.
Smithsonian National Zoo, lemurs.
WWF, Madagascar.
n.certNote: Scientists agree Madagascar's animals evolved in isolation. How the ancestors of lemurs and other mammals first got there, probably by rafting across the sea, is still debated, and so is exactly when the first people arrived.

sec.h: Lemurs, fossas and a finger like a twig
sec.t:
Lemurs are primates, related to monkeys, apes and us, but from a much older branch. They range from the mouse lemur, which fits in your palm, to the indri, which sings loud wailing songs through the rainforest. Ring-tailed lemurs sunbathe in the morning with their arms spread wide.

The aye-aye taps on tree bark with a long, thin middle finger, listens for grubs moving inside, then hooks them out. The fossa, which looks like a cross between a cat and a mongoose, is the island's top hunter and climbs trees after lemurs.

Chameleons here come in every size, from one of the smallest [[reptile|reptiles]] on Earth, about as long as a fingernail, to giants longer than a ruler. Their colour changes and [[@camouflage|camouflage]] help them signal to each other and hide from birds.

Humans reached Madagascar surprisingly late, probably in the last few thousand years, though the exact timing is debated. Some of the first settlers sailed all the way from Southeast Asia, across the Indian Ocean. Others came from Africa. That is why the Malagasy language is related to languages spoken in Borneo, thousands of kilometres away, while many people also have African ancestry.

People found giant animals that are now gone. Elephant birds, taller than a man and flightless, laid eggs that could hold the contents of more than a hundred hen's eggs. They and giant lemurs the size of gorillas died out within the last thousand years or so, much like the [[@dodo|dodo]] on nearby Mauritius.

Much of Madagascar's original forest has been cut down, for farming, firewood and charcoal. Many lemurs are now [[endangered|endangered]], and some kinds live in only a single patch of forest. Scientists warn that the island is one of the places on Earth where [[@extinction-today|extinction]] is happening fastest. When forest is cleared on steep hills, rain washes the red soil into the rivers, which run rusty red into the sea. Astronauts have described seeing that red stain from [[orbit|orbit]]. National parks and local groups are working to protect what remains.

text: The Hajj is a [[pilgrimage|pilgrimage]], a religious journey, to the city of Mecca in Saudi Arabia. It is one of the five pillars of Islam, the basic duties of a Muslim. Every adult Muslim who is healthy enough and can afford it is expected to go at least once in their life.

The Hajj takes place over five or six days each year, in the Islamic month of Dhul Hijjah. Pilgrims follow a set of [[ritual|rituals]] in and around Mecca that remember the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), his wife Hajar and their son Ismail. In 2024 about 1.8 million people took part, from almost every country on Earth. Only Muslims are allowed to enter Mecca.

st.prompt: During the Hajj, men wear just two pieces of plain white unstitched cloth. Why?

options.t: So that rich and poor, kings and farmers, all look the same before God
Because coloured clothes are not sold in Mecca
To keep their clothes from getting dusty

st.reveal: The special state of purity on the Hajj is called ihram, and the simple clothing is part of it. No one can tell who is a prince and who is a labourer. Women also dress simply and modestly, often in white, but do not have to wear the two cloths.

sec.t:
At the heart of Mecca's Great Mosque stands the Kaaba, a cube-shaped stone building about 15 metres high, draped in black cloth embroidered with gold verses from the [[@quran-intro|Quran]]. Muslims believe Ibrahim and Ismail built it as a house for the worship of one God.

Five times a day, Muslims all over the world turn towards the Kaaba to pray. In India, that means facing roughly west. In the USA it means facing north-east. On arriving, pilgrims walk around the Kaaba seven times, anticlockwise, in a ritual called tawaf. Seen from above, the crowd moves like a slow white whirlpool.

The Hajj ends with Eid al-Adha, the festival of sacrifice. It remembers the story of Ibrahim's readiness to sacrifice his son at God's command, and the ram sent in his place. Families who can afford it share meat from an animal with relatives, neighbours and people in need. Muslims around the world, including those who are not on Hajj, celebrate the same [[@eid|Eid]], which Indians often call Bakrid.

Because the Islamic calendar follows the [[@moon-phases|Moon]], its year is about 354 days long. That is why Eid and the Hajj come about 11 days earlier each year in the usual [[@calendars|calendar]].

People have travelled to Mecca for centuries, by camel [[caravan|caravan]], ship and on foot. In 1325, a 21-year-old from [[@morocco|Morocco]] named [[@ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]] set off for the Hajj. He kept going for nearly 30 years and reached India, China and East Africa.

A year earlier, in 1324, [[@ancient-africa|Mansa Musa]], the ruler of the Mali Empire in West Africa, crossed the Sahara on his way to Mecca with a vast caravan. Writers of the time said he handed out so much gold in [[@world-cairo|Cairo]] that its value there dropped for years.

Today, most pilgrims fly. India sends one of the largest groups, more than a lakh of pilgrims in recent years. Saudi Arabia has built huge tented camps at Mina, cooling sprays and wide walkways, since moving so many people safely through summer heat that can pass 45°C is an enormous task.

text: In India, mustard is a seed, an oil, a vegetable and a sauce. Tiny black or brown seeds crackle in hot oil at the start of countless dals and curries. [[@oils-cooking|Mustard oil]] is the main cooking oil in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Assam, Punjab and much of Uttar Pradesh. The leaves become sarson ka saag in Punjab. In Bengal, ground mustard turns into a sharp paste for fish.
India is one of the world's biggest growers of mustard. In winter, fields across the north turn bright yellow with its flowers.

st.prompt: Dry mustard seeds taste mild. What makes ground mustard suddenly hot and sharp?

options.t: Water mixing with the crushed seeds
Heating the seeds until they burn
Adding salt

st.reveal: Crushing the seeds lets an enzyme meet another chemical stored separately in the seed. With water, they react to make a sharp-tasting oil. Heat actually weakens it, which is why mustard seeds fried in a tadka taste nutty, not fiery.

sec.t:
In south and west India, mustard seeds (called *rai*, *kadugu* or *mohari*) go into almost every tadka, or tempering. They are dropped into hot oil until they pop and crackle, often with [[@curry-leaves|curry leaves]], cumin and dried chillies. Then the whole spoonful is poured over dal, sambar, poha or a vegetable.

Frying in oil makes the seeds nutty instead of hot. That's because the sharp taste only forms when crushed seeds meet water, which produces a sharp chemical called allyl isothiocyanate. Heat destroys the [[enzyme|enzyme]] that starts that reaction.

In Bengal and Odisha, mustard is ground with water into a paste that can make your eyes water. [[@bengali-food|Bengali]] cooks use it in *shorshe ilish*, hilsa fish steamed or cooked in mustard sauce, one of the region's most loved dishes. *Kasundi*, a fermented Bengali mustard sauce, is eaten with fried snacks and is now sold in jars around the world.

Raw mustard oil is strong and pungent too. Cooks often heat it until it smokes slightly to mellow it before adding spices. Many families in the north also use mustard oil for [[@pickles-achar|pickles]]. Mango, lemon and chilli pickles sit in jars of it for months, because the oil and spices help keep the vegetables from spoiling.

In Punjab, the leaves are as important as the seeds. *Sarson ka saag*, slow-cooked mustard greens, is eaten in winter with makki di roti, flatbread made of maize, and a lump of white butter.

Mustard oil is also used outside the kitchen. In many north Indian homes, babies get a warm mustard oil massage, and the oil is rubbed into hair. In winter, some people put a drop in their nostrils, an old home custom.

In the USA, mustard usually means a bright yellow sauce squeezed onto hot dogs. It is made from milder white mustard seeds, vinegar and turmeric, which gives the colour. France is famous for Dijon mustard, made with brown seeds and wine or vinegar. Germany and England have their own versions.

American rules limit a fatty [[acid|acid]] called erucic acid in food, and traditional mustard oil contains a lot of it. So in the USA, mustard oil is often sold labelled "for external use only". Scientists still debate how much it matters for people's health. Meanwhile, Indian scientists have bred new mustard varieties with less erucic acid. Canola, popular in North America, came from breeding the same family of plants.
